title: Removal disputes before Myers
summary: The source traces competing claims about removal through the First Congress, early party turnover, Jackson’s bank dispute, and Johnson’s impeachment.
notes:
The Decision of 1789 substituted language presupposing presidential removal for an express grant in the Foreign Affairs legislation. Taft later treated this as recognition of constitutional power, while the editors report historical disagreement over whether the episode resolves its source or scope. The Jefferson transition illustrates partisan removal and the complications of appointment completion; the Marbury discussion distinguishes its historical fixed-term statement from later interpretations of terms of office.

Jackson removed Treasury Secretary Duane after Duane refused to transfer deposits from the national bank, producing conflicting congressional reactions and a Senate censure later expunged. The Tenure in Office Act constrained Andrew Johnson’s ability to remove officers, and his attempt to remove Stanton triggered impeachment; acquittal by one vote did not settle every removal question. The later repeal of that Act coexisted with newly enacted commission protections and the postmaster restriction challenged in Myers. Political practice therefore supplies arguments and context, while these episodes do not function as a uniform judicial holding.
